title: The Science of Sound
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Sound is a form of energy that travels through the air as a wave. When something vibrates, such as a guitar string or a loudspeaker, it pushes the air around it, creating areas where the air is squeezed together and areas where it is stretched apart. These changes of pressure spread outwards in all directions and reach the ear, where they are converted into signals for the brain. Because sound is carried by matter, it cannot travel through a vacuum, which is why there is no sound in space.

Scientists describe sound waves by two main properties. The first is frequency, the number of vibrations in each second, measured in hertz. A high frequency produces a high note, and a low frequency a low one. A human ear can hear frequencies from about 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz, though the upper limit falls with age. Dogs hear sounds up to about 45,000 hertz, and bats and dolphins can detect even higher frequencies, which they use to find their way and their food in the dark or in murky water.

The second property is amplitude, the height of the wave, which determines how loud a sound is. A large amplitude means that the air is pushed hard, and the sound is loud, while a small amplitude gives a quiet sound. Loudness is measured in decibels. A whisper is about 30 decibels, normal conversation about 60, and a rock concert more than 100. Sounds above 85 decibels can damage hearing if they are heard for many hours, and very loud sounds can cause harm in a few minutes.

Sound travels at different speeds in different materials. In air at room temperature the speed is about 343 metres per second, which is roughly 1,200 kilometres an hour. In water it is more than four times faster, and in steel about fifteen times faster, since the particles are closer together and pass on the vibration more quickly. This is why a person can hear a train coming by putting an ear to the rail long before the sound arrives through the air. The difference between the speed of light and that of sound also explains why we see lightning before we hear thunder.

When a sound wave meets a hard surface, it bounces back as an echo. If the surface is more than about seventeen metres away, the echo comes back late enough to be heard as a separate sound. Bats and dolphins use echoes to find their way: they send out a series of high-pitched clicks and listen to the returning echoes, which tell them how far away an object is. Ships use a similar device, called sonar, to measure the depth of the sea and to find submarines and shoals of fish.

Music depends on regular vibrations. Each instrument produces a particular mixture of frequencies, which gives it its own character, called timbre; this is why a violin and a flute can play the same note yet sound completely different. In string instruments the pitch depends on the length, thickness and tension of the string. A shorter string vibrates faster and gives a higher note, which is why a guitarist presses a string against the fingerboard to shorten the part that vibrates.

Not all sounds are welcome, and unwanted sound is called noise. In cities, traffic, building work and aircraft produce noise that can cause stress, poor sleep and even heart disease. Dr Lena Fischer, an acoustic engineer, says that noise is among the most underestimated forms of pollution. Cities can reduce it by using quieter road surfaces, by planting trees and by building walls beside busy roads. Individuals can protect themselves with earplugs, and by turning down the volume of their headphones.
